I want the faster one, and I have no problems integrating both at the same time The SIGILL issue seems to be something very nasty really that will bite everyone randomly According to an upstream bugreport, 25% of cloud VMs will run CPUs that crash (unless you shell out for really high env VMs)\ I don't think it will be acceptable to have KZG crash randomly at runtime We *really* should have that fixed before shipping it out Extremely strongly suggest fixing that I am the plan for Geth and I hve yet to see which library is better. For now, both have blocking shrotcomings Note, my fit now is not that this issue exists, that's natural and I opened a bugreport. My very serious fit is that this was a known issue and everyone was like "myeah, we don't care". How can such a thing happen? What’s the blocking shortcoming of the pure golang version? https://github.com/crate-crypto/go-kzg-4844/issues/44 I can look into this now -- exposing that parameter should not be hard -- let me know if any other issues arise I've released a 0.1.2 that you can use which by default sets the number of go routines to 1 and allows you to set it to a different number via an exposed function Seems that's not enough, the underlying lib that go-kzg uses does not honour its own concurrency config it goes ahead and spins up goroutines anyway for certain operations, even if configured not to <@555483069038198827> feel free to name this situation appropriately since you didn't like me calling it a shitshow 😛 <dankrad> a missing feature? <dankrad> is spinning up goroutines in any way a danger? worst case it just wastes some resources, right? performance is unpredictable Running it on "1 thread" takes 6.7ms, running it on "20 threads" takes 6ms <dankrad> so? it highlights that it's threading is mostly moot and I can't disable it nor control it to be more meaningful I don't like it when a low level library makes high level decisions, expecially when those are wrong <dankrad> your numbers feel wrong, what operation is this for? I would be very surprised if you can compute a commitment in 6.7 ms on one thread hence why I placed them in quotation marks 🙂 becuse you cannot control it from the outside the numbers are arbitrary rollercoasters you cannot meaningfully measure it, nor optimise with it, nor figure out what's the best way for your specific use case the library makes internal decisions on something it should not <dankrad> fair enough. You are running in open doors here, I also like to get single thread numbers for benchmarks. Still it works and I don't see an obvious problem for the user. <dankrad> You have made your feature request and it's going to get implemented, what more do you want? It needs rto be implemented in gnark-crypto because that's what's broken and designing it will be extremely hard because of how the code is architected so no, it won't get implemented, trust me <dankrad> that seems unlikely, that it is so hard to implement disabling concurrency? maybe someone will hack it in. making it fully configurable so that you can optimise for it? I'm not even sure how you can model that to meaningfully configure implementing it is probably trivial, designing the config meaningfully is probably hard surprise me I guess 😛 I just don't see anyone putting the effort into it - to truly elegantly do it - and get it upstreamed, sorry <dankrad> what about simply having two functions so you can choose between concurrency or no? Seems fine to me <dankrad> alternatively specify number of threads as a param <dankrad> like I just don't see your behaviour here as very constructive "Hey, I want the library to behave like this. Haha and by the way what I want is actually impossible so deal with it" <dankrad> I would love to have more constructive discussions with you on how to make the libraries better, ideally back in January and not now. I guess that would be the advantage of doing something hacky first, so that you can find out about these things. Ah yes, sure. I would also prefer not to have to write production code and be able to yolo my whole fucking life, wouldn't it be grant Oh, hope you remember all those things we said to you last year about Verkel Because we did tell you where it fails and what won't work and the perf issues Just so you don't tell me in a year that you didn't know peace out <dankrad> but you were not open to understanding how your objections could be resolved. When we talked about some of the details that you claimed were impossible to solve, we did actually find solutions <dankrad> it's an iterative process This is a public complain for BLST everywhere, we rolled out our own hashing assembly with CPU detection instead of bothering trying to open PRs to them in part because of this. I don't really understand how this piece of software that was funded in large part by the EF (AFAIK) has this feature that multiple coredevs from multiple teams asked them to do and they still managed to ignore these requests we have had several validators crashing when we defaulted to BSLT + ADX, we had to revert it and by it not being default I suspect that the vast majority of prysm nodes run a really underperforming BLS signature verification library Is not that we didn't care, the first request was before mainnet launch https://github.com/supranational/blst/issues/10 and every single team requested this. Surely enough, soon we started crashing on runtime https://github.com/supranational/blst/issues/31 But what can we do, options are we either roll out our own assembly (as we did with SHA256) or we have to take it. At least now we have Gnark to test with. Although in my personal computers it benchmarks slower than BLST.

excerpts.author: potuz
excerpts.content: This is a public complain for BLST everywhere, we rolled out our own hashing assembly with CPU detection instead of bothering trying to open PRs to them in part because of this.

excerpts.author: potuz
excerpts.content: I don't really understand how this piece of software that was funded in large part by the EF (AFAIK) has this feature that multiple coredevs from multiple teams asked them to do and they still managed to ignore these requests

excerpts.author: potuz
excerpts.content: we have had several validators crashing when we defaulted to BSLT + ADX, we had to revert it and by it not being default I suspect that the vast majority of prysm nodes run a really underperforming BLS signature verification library

excerpts.author: potuz
excerpts.content:
Is not that we didn't care, the first request was before mainnet launch https://github.com/supranational/blst/issues/10  and every single team requested this. Surely enough, soon we started crashing on runtime https://github.com/supranational/blst/issues/31 
But what can we do, options are we either roll out our own assembly (as we did with SHA256) or we have to take it. At least now we have Gnark to test with. Although in my personal computers it benchmarks slower than BLST.
